_slice: Texas and Houston — the counter-sample to California and Los Angeles
_note: Built from research Grok produced against a brief, then put through a citation-resolution pass because roughly two in five of its evidence_url fields were pointers rather than documents — "TEA school finance pages", "PSF / SBOE materials", "TRS reports". The structure it proposed held up; several of its specifics did not, and the corrections are recorded in _dropped rather than quietly fixed. Texas answers the same questions as California and answers them differently almost everywhere. California caps what a property is worth and lets the rate float; Texas caps what a jurisdiction may charge and lets the value float. California's counties appraise; Texas hands appraisal to independent districts and then has the state audit them, and the audited value rather than the local one drives school funding — the Property Value Study has no California equivalent at all. California legislates against five different price indexes; Texas mostly does not legislate against price indexes, preferring property value growth and fixed historical baselines, and the clearest exception is local: Houston's revenue cap, which reads a Houston-area CPI and a federal population estimate. The one structure that transfers cleanly is the pension chain — experience study, valuation, contribution rate, budget — and even there the two Texas systems differ, since the teacher system's current valuation is running on assumptions four years old while the state employee system's is in phase.

reports.title: Consumer Price Index, Houston-The Woodlands-Sugar Land
reports.publisher: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Southwest Information Office
reports.description: The metropolitan-area CPI-U for the Houston core based statistical area, and the index the City of Houston uses to adjust its property tax revenue cap. Published bimonthly rather than monthly, in even months, and not seasonally adjusted. The area has been renamed twice — from Houston-Galveston-Brazoria, and again under the 2023 delineation — while the underlying series identifier stayed put.
reports.cadence_note: Bimonthly, which matters less than it looks: the City reads the annual average for the preceding calendar year, so a six-a-year series still yields a usable yearly figure.

release_schedule.note: BLS Southwest Information Office publishes Houston-The Woodlands-Sugar Land CPI bimonthly (every other month: Feb, Apr, Jun, Aug, Oct, Dec), consistent with releases_per_year=6 on file. The July 14, 2026 news release (covering June 2026 data) explicitly states the next release date.

reports.title: Texas Tax Code Chapter 26 — Assessment and Truth-in-Taxation
reports.description: The statutory machinery every Texas taxing unit runs each year: the chief appraiser certifies the appraisal roll, the assessor computes the no-new-revenue tax rate and the voter-approval tax rate, and a rate above the voter-approval rate requires an election. Texas's answer to the question California answers with Proposition 13, and a completely different answer — a cap on the rate rather than on the value.

reports.title: Texas Tax Code §23.23 — Limitation on Appraised Value of Residence Homestead
reports.description: The one broad value cap in Texas law: a homestead's appraised value may not exceed the lesser of market value or the prior year's appraised value plus 10 percent plus the market value of new improvements. Narrower than Proposition 13 in three ways — it applies only to homesteads, it caps appraised rather than market value so market value keeps being determined underneath it, and it expires when the qualifying owner does.

reports.title: Texas Government Code §403.302 — Determination of School District Property Values
reports.description: The mandate for the Comptroller's study of school district property values. The provision that lets a state agency substitute its own valuation for a local appraisal district's when the local one fails an audit, for the purpose of distributing state education money.

reports.title: Texas Constitution Article III §49-g — Economic Stabilization Fund
reports.description: The constitutional formula transferring oil and gas production tax revenue above fiscal 1987 levels into the Economic Stabilization Fund, splitting the result with the State Highway Fund, and capping the fund's balance at 10 percent of the preceding biennium's general revenue deposits.

reports.title: Texas Constitution Article VII §5 — Permanent School Fund distribution
reports.description: The total-return rule governing what the Permanent School Fund may distribute to the Available School Fund: not more than 6 percent of the average market value of the fund on the last day of each of the 16 state fiscal quarters preceding the regular legislative session before the biennium, subject to a 10-year total-return ceiling.

reports.title: Water District Financial Management Guide
reports.description: The accounting and audit framework Texas water districts — including the municipal utility districts that finance suburban Houston — keep their records under. The counterpart in this corpus to GASB's standards, but for a class of special district that has no equivalent anywhere else in the graph.

reports.title: School District Property Value Study
reports.publisher: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts, Property Tax Assistance Division
reports.description: The state's independent ratio study of taxable property value in every school district, conducted at least once every two years using comparable sales and audit sampling, and certified to the Commissioner of Education for use in school funding. The structure with no California equivalent: a state agency audits local appraisals, and where the local value fails the audit the state value is used instead — so the number that drives the money is not necessarily the one the appraisal district produced.

release_schedule.rule: Tax Code Sec. 5.10 / Gov't Code Sec. 403.302 require the comptroller to conduct the property value study at least once every two years, but in practice the Comptroller runs the School District PVS annually: "In December, our office releases local data and values for the sampled properties... we release the preliminary School District PVS findings at the end of January" (certified to the Commissioner of Education), followed by final findings certified after the 40-day protest period, which historically has landed in mid-to-late August of the following year (e.g. 2022 study final findings certified Aug. 24, 2023; 2023 study final findings certified Aug. 15, 2024; 2024 study final findings certified Aug. 15, 2025).

entries.covers: 2025 tax-year School District PVS final findings certification to the Commissioner of Education (not yet posted as of 2026-08-11; the 2025 preliminary findings were certified Jan. 30, 2026, and prior years' final findings have consistently followed in mid-to-late August)
2026 tax-year School District PVS preliminary findings certification to the Commissioner of Education (per the Comptroller's stated 'end of January' release pattern)

release_schedule.note: Historical record on the Comptroller's site (2016-2025) shows the study actually runs annually, not biennially: every tax year has both preliminary findings (certified end of January of the following year) and final findings (certified mid-to-late August, sometimes with staggered later certifications for individual districts still under review, e.g. 2022 study had certifications trailing into 2024). This suggests the corpus's releases_per_year=0.5 (biennial) understates the actual annual cadence.

reports.title: Foundation School Program state funding
reports.description: The core school funding system — basic allotment, Tier One entitlement, tax rate compression and the recapture of local revenue above entitlement. Recapture, in which a property-wealthy district sends local tax revenue back to the state for redistribution, has no analogue anywhere else in this corpus.
reports.cadence_note: Revised continuously across the school year rather than published on a fixed calendar: six-week attendance updates under HB 2, LPE/DPE milestone revisions (≈March and July), and a post-session settle-up. Nominal 6/year reflects the six-week reporting rhythm. Corrected from 1/year on 2026-08-12 — Thomas's Q3 ruling, from TEA's own timeline showing a multi-stage cycle of roughly 4–6 updates per year.

entries.covers: FY2025-26 FSP Near-Final Summary of Finances update (summer attendance data)
FY2025-26 FSP Near-Final Summary of Finances update (Tax Information Survey / annual financial report data)
FY2025-26 FSP Final Summary of Finances settle-up (debt service, excess collections, ADA)

release_schedule.rule: TEA's Foundation School Program (FSP) Summary of Finances (SOF) funding reports follow a stated annual update cycle: the Legislative Payment Estimate (LPE) is initially released in the Fall, updated in February/March with current-year fall attendance data, and further updated in May/July as additional attendance data (4th/5th six-weeks ADA and FTEs) becomes available. Near-Final reports are then updated in September (incorporating summer attendance data) and again in October/November as Tax Information Survey data and districts' annual financial reports become available. Final reports are updated in April/May of the following year 'based on eligible debt service, excess collections, and ADA' — the settle-up stage.
release_schedule.note: TEA does not publish FSP funding as a single dated annual release; instead, per-district Summary of Finances funding data (LPE, DPE, Near-Final, Final) is revised on a recurring multi-stage cycle throughout each school year and into the following spring, as documented in TEA's 'Data Elements, Sources, and Timelines for FSP SOF Reports' (dated Feb 2026). No exact calendar dates are published — only named periods (e.g. 'September', 'October/November', 'April/May') — so entries above use month-level precision for the next few stages of the cycle in progress as of 2026-08-11.

reports.title: Maximum Compressed Tax Rates letter to administrators
reports.description: The annual letter telling every school district the maximum maintenance and operations rate it may compress to, computed from state-certified property value growth. Structurally the twin of California's Board of Equalization letter to county assessors: one short annual document, addressed to every local unit at once, that sets a rate the whole state then runs on.

entries.covers: Tax Year 2026 Final Maximum Compressed Tax Rates (MCR) and Adoption of Tax Rate letter

release_schedule.note: No published calendar or statutory deadline was found for this specific TAA letter. Past editions were issued at a consistent time of year, in the final week of August (occasionally spilling into September 1): TY2022 final letter dated 2022-09-01, TY2024 final letter dated 2024-08-29, TY2025 final letter dated 2025-08-28. TEA also issues a separate 'Preliminary MCR' letter earlier each summer (e.g., TY2025 preliminary letter dated 2025-08-05, and a TY2025 letter dated 2025-06-12), which this corpus entry (the FINAL letter) follows. The projected 2026-08 entry is an inference from this observed pattern, not a published date.

reports.title: Biennial Revenue Estimate
reports.description: The constitutionally required estimate of revenue available for the coming two-year budget period. Appropriations exceeding it are invalid without a four-fifths vote of both chambers, and no appropriation bill reaches the Governor without the Comptroller's certificate that it fits inside the estimate. A forecast with legal force, which the California budget documents do not have.

entries.covers: Biennial Revenue Estimate for the 2028-29 biennium, submitted at the convening of the 90th Texas Legislature

release_schedule.rule: It shall be the duty of the Comptroller of Public Accounts in advance of each Regular Session of the Legislature to prepare and submit to the Governor and to the Legislature upon its convening a statement under oath showing fully the financial condition of the State Treasury at the close of the last fiscal period and an estimate of the probable receipts and disbursements for the then current fiscal year and the succeeding biennium. (Texas Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 49a)
release_schedule.note: The Texas Legislature meets in regular session only in odd-numbered years, convening on the second Tuesday in January (Texas Constitution Art. III, Sec. 5). The BRE is constitutionally required to be submitted at that convening. In practice the Comptroller has released it the day before or on the convening date (e.g., Jan 13, 2025 for the session convening Jan 14, 2025; Jan 7, 2019 for session convening Jan 8, 2019). The next regular session convenes Jan 12, 2027, so the next BRE (covering FY2028-29) is expected on or about that date; no calendar page with a confirmed exact release date has been published yet as of Aug 2026.

reports.title: Certification Revenue Estimate
reports.description: The updated revenue estimate issued after a legislative session, against which the Comptroller certifies the appropriations actually passed. The enforcement step the Biennial Revenue Estimate only sets up.

entries.covers: 2026-27 biennium Certification Revenue Estimate (most recent, released by Acting Comptroller Kelly Hancock)
2028-29 biennium Certification Revenue Estimate (projected, following conclusion of the 2027 regular legislative session)

release_schedule.note: The Certification Revenue Estimate (CRE) is issued once per biennium, after the Texas Legislature's regular session (and any special sessions) concludes, to certify that the General Appropriations Act and other appropriations bills are within available revenue, per Texas Government Code Sec. 403.0131. It follows the Biennial Revenue Estimate (BRE) issued before each regular session. No fixed statutory date exists for the CRE -- observed release dates cluster in fall of odd-numbered years (Oct-Nov), shortly after the session (including any special sessions) ends. The next edition (for the 2028-29 biennium) would be expected in fall 2027, after the 2027 regular session concludes, but the exact date depends on when the legislature finishes its work.

reports.title: Monthly State Revenue Watch
reports.description: Monthly cash-basis reporting of state revenue by source, including net oil and natural gas production tax collections — the series the Economic Stabilization Fund transfer is computed against.

entries.covers: August 2026 revenue/sales tax collections (projected next update)

release_schedule.note: The Comptroller's own page states 'These reports are updated monthly' but provides no fixed calendar or specific day-of-month rule. Observed historical releases (both the Revenue Watch data page updates and the closely tied 'State Sales Tax Revenue' news releases covering the same monthly collections data) consistently land within the first 1-3 business days of each month, reporting the prior month's collections. Based on this pattern, the next update covering August 2026 collections is expected in the first few days of September 2026. Confirmed release dates found: 2023-09-01, 2024-09-03, 2025-09-03, 2026-04-01, 2026-05-01, 2026-08-03.

reports.title: Economic Stabilization Fund and State Highway Fund severance tax transfers
reports.description: The annual computation and execution of the constitutional transfers of oil and gas production tax revenue into the Economic Stabilization Fund and the State Highway Fund. As of the 2026-27 estimate the fund has reached its constitutional ceiling, so the highway fund keeps its share while the stabilization fund's falls to zero in 2027 and the remainder goes to general revenue.

entries.covers: FY2026 severance tax transfer to ESF and State Highway Fund

release_schedule.rule: Texas Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 49-g(c): "Not later than the 90th day of each fiscal year, the comptroller of public accounts shall transfer" the constitutionally determined amounts (including 75% of oil and gas production tax collections in excess of the 1987 baseline, split between the Economic Stabilization Fund and the State Highway Fund) from the prior fiscal year. Texas's fiscal year ends August 31, so the deadline falls on approximately November 29 each year; the Comptroller has historically announced the transfer around that date (e.g., Nov. 26, 2024; Nov. 30, 2023; Nov. 29, 2022; Nov. 30, 2021).
release_schedule.note: The 90th day after the August 31 fiscal-year-end is computed here as November 29, 2026; the Comptroller's actual announcement date in past years has landed within a few days of this constitutional deadline (sometimes slightly before it, e.g. Nov. 26 in 2024). The corpus URL (comptroller.texas.gov/economy/fiscal-notes/government/2025/esf-info/) is a general informational/explainer page about the ESF, not a dated calendar; the actual dated announcements are published as individual Comptroller press releases each November (e.g. the 2024 transfer release), which are not a single stable landing page.

reports.title: Permanent School Fund distribution rate to the Available School Fund
reports.description: The distribution rate the State Board of Education adopts each biennium, moving investment returns and land and mineral royalties from the Permanent School Fund into the Available School Fund and thence to schools. Since 2023 the fund itself is managed by a separate Permanent School Fund Corporation, leaving the rate decision with the Board.

entries.covers: PSF-to-ASF distribution rate for the 2028-29 state fiscal biennium

release_schedule.rule: Tex. Const. art. VII, sec. 5(a)(1)(A): the State Board of Education, by a vote of two-thirds of its total membership taken before the regular session of the legislature convenes, determines the rate of distribution (as a percentage of the average market value of the Permanent School Fund) to the Available School Fund for the succeeding state fiscal biennium. The distribution may not exceed six percent of the fund's average market value over the preceding sixteen state fiscal quarters (and, per the 10-year total-return test reviewed annually by SBOE, may not exceed the fund's 10-year total investment return).
release_schedule.note: SBOE must set the rate before the Texas Legislature's next regular session convenes (2nd Tuesday of January in odd years — Jan 12, 2027). Observed past rate-setting actions occurred Aug 31, 2022 (for 2024-25 biennium) and Nov 22, 2024 (for 2026-27 biennium, rate 3.45%, ~$1.8B/year), i.e. in the fall of the preceding even year, consistent with the 0.5/year (biennial) cadence already on file. Exact 2026 meeting date not yet published as of 2026-08-11. Separately, SBOE conducts an annual (not biennial) compliance review each September/fall confirming the 6% and 10-year tests still permit distributions to continue within an already-adopted biennial rate (e.g. September 2025 Committee on School Finance/PSF Item 2).

reports.title: Transit District Sales and Use Tax allocation
reports.description: The monthly allocation of transit authority sales and use tax collections back to each authority, net of the state's 2 percent service charge. The channel through which a Houston retail sale becomes transit revenue.

release_schedule.note: The Comptroller publishes a single 'Sales Tax Allocation Payment Distribution Schedule' covering all local sales/use tax allocations (cities, counties, special purpose districts, metropolitan transit authorities, and city transit departments), including the Transit District Sales and Use Tax allocation. Payments are monthly, consistent with releases_per_year=12 on file.

reports.title: TRS Actuarial Valuation Report
reports.description: The annual valuation of the Teacher Retirement System, setting funded status and contribution requirements as of each August 31.

entries.covers: FY2024 (valuation date Aug 31, 2024) actuarial valuation report - certification letter
FY2025 (valuation date Aug 31, 2025) actuarial valuation report - certification letter
FY2026 (valuation date Aug 31, 2026) actuarial valuation report - expected certification/board presentation

release_schedule.note: TRS publishes an annual actuarial valuation report as of each fiscal year end (August 31). Based on the 2024 and 2025 editions, the actuary's certification letter is issued in mid-to-late November, and the full report (document plus PowerPoint) is presented to the TRS Board in December of the same year. No published fixed calendar or statutory deadline was found; this is inferred from the consistent pattern across the archive of reports (annual editions found for 2014-2025).

reports.title: TRS Actuarial Experience Study
reports.description: The four-yearly study of actual system experience against the standing assumptions, recommending the demographic and economic assumptions the valuations then use.

release_schedule.note: TRS conducts an actuarial experience study roughly every 3-4 years, tied to the actuarial valuation cycle, but there is no published calendar or codified fixed-interval rule found. Past editions found: 2015, 2018 (issued 2018-07-27), 2022 (issued 2022-07-15), and 2026 (issued 2026-02-06, already released before today's date of 2026-08-11). Gaps have been 3, 4, and ~3.6 years respectively, so the next edition is estimated to arrive around 2029-2030 rather than on a fixed date.

reports.title: ERS Actuarial Valuation Reports
reports.description: The annual valuation of the pension plans administered by the Employees Retirement System, covering the main plan, the law enforcement and custodial officer fund and the judicial retirement plan.

entries.covers: Pension actuarial valuation as of August 31, 2026

release_schedule.note: The ERS reports page lists no fixed release calendar or stated statutory deadline. Instead it shows a consistent multi-year pattern: the annual pension actuarial valuation is performed as of the fiscal year end (August 31) and the full 'ERS Pension Valuation Reports' document is published in December of the same calendar year (Dec 2024, Dec 2023, Dec 2022, Dec 2021, Dec 2020), with a companion OPEB valuation report typically published in November of the same year and a pension valuation summary in Nov/Dec. As of this check (2026-08-11), the page's most recent posted edition is still the 2024 valuation (Dec 2024) - no 2025 edition was visible on the page, so the FY2025 (Aug 31, 2025) valuation may be posted late or the page may lag actual publication. The next expected release per the observed pattern is the FY2026 valuation (as of Aug 31, 2026), expected around December 2026.

reports.title: ERS Actuarial Experience Study
reports.description: The four-yearly experience investigation from which the Board of Trustees adopts the assumptions used in subsequent valuations.

entries.covers: Next ERS Actuarial Experience Study (statutorily due at least once every 4 years after the March 2024 study)

release_schedule.rule: At least once every four years, the actuary, under the direction of the board of trustees, shall make an actuarial investigation of the mortality, service, and compensation experience of the members and beneficiaries of the retirement system (Tex. Gov't Code Sec. 815.206(c)).
release_schedule.note: The most recent study (covering the 4-year period ending August 31, 2023) was presented to the ERS Board on March 20, 2024, following the same cadence as the prior study (period ending August 31, 2020, presented as a March 2020 board presentation with a May 2020 final report). Texas Government Code Sec. 815.206(c) requires an experience investigation at least once every four years, so the next one is due by 2028; the March 2028 date is projected from the observed 4-year cadence (March 2020 -> March 2024) rather than a published calendar.

reports.title: Harris Central Appraisal District Annual Appraisal Roll
reports.description: The annual roll of appraised value for all taxable property in Harris County, valued as of January 1 and certified to the assessor for each taxing unit. Note what is unusual by California standards: the appraisal district is its own entity with its own board, not an office of the county.

release_schedule.rule: The chief appraiser shall prepare and certify to the assessor for each taxing unit ... that part of the appraisal roll for the district that lists the property taxable by the unit, by July 25 (Tex. Tax Code §26.01(a)).
release_schedule.note: 2026-07-25 has already passed as of this audit (2026-08-11). Harris Central actually certified on 16 August in 2024, so the statutory date is a floor rather than a guarantee — see the reference_period note on the outbound dependency edges.

reports.title: City of Houston property tax revenue cap calculation
reports.description: The annual computation of the ceiling on the City's property tax revenue under the 2004 charter amendment, as amended in 2006 to add $90 million for public safety. The limit is the lesser of the prior year's collections plus 4.5 percent, or the fiscal 2005 base adjusted cumulatively for inflation and population growth. The closest structural analogue in the corpus to California's Gann limit, and it reaches a different answer: a local price index and a federal population estimate rather than a state personal income measure.

entries.covers: FY2027 property tax revenue cap calculation, presented to City Council ahead of the FY2027 tax rate adoption

release_schedule.note: The City of Houston Finance Department presents its property tax revenue cap calculation (under Props 1 and H, and SB2) to the City Council Budget and Fiscal Affairs (BFA) Committee annually in the fall, timed to the annual property tax rate adoption process (Houston's fiscal year runs July 1-June 30). Confirmed past instances: 'COH Revenue Cap Presentation' on 2021-09-07 (https://www.houstontx.gov/council/committees/bfacommittee/20210907/revenue-cap.pdf) and 'Property Tax Update, COH Revenue Cap' on 2025-10-07 (https://www.houstontx.gov/council/committees/bfacommittee/20251007/revenue-cap.pdf), the latter coinciding with the FY2026 tax-rate decision reported in the press. No dedicated release calendar was found for this specific document; only these two dated instances of the BFA presentation were located, so the projected FY2027 window (Sept-Oct 2026) is inferred rather than certain.

reports.title: City of Houston Adopted Budget
reports.description: The City's annual operating and capital budget for the fiscal year beginning July 1, carrying the revenue cap computation and the property tax revenue estimate that follows from it.

release_schedule.note: No published multi-year release calendar or single stated statutory deadline date was found on the City's site; however, Houston's fiscal year runs July 1 - June 30, and City Council has consistently adopted the annual budget in early-to-mid June each year (FY2025: June 12, 2024; FY2026: June 4, 2025; FY2027: June 10, 2026), just ahead of the new fiscal year's start. Next adoption (for FY2028) is projected for June 2027 based on this pattern; exact date not yet published.

reports.title: City of Houston Annual Comprehensive Financial Report
reports.description: The City's audited annual financial statements for the fiscal year ended June 30, whose first note is where the revenue cap is described in the terms the bond market relies on.

release_schedule.note: No published release calendar or codified statutory deadline was found on the Controller's site. However, the transmittal-letter dates on the last three published ACFR PDFs show a consistent pattern: the report for the fiscal year ended June 30 is issued in November or December of the same calendar year (roughly 4.5-6 months after fiscal year end), consistent with GFOA best-practice guidance of issuance within ~180 days of fiscal year end. Next expected release is the FY2026 ACFR (fiscal year ended June 30, 2026), projected for Q4 2026 based on this pattern.

reports.title: Harris County Adopted Budget
reports.description: The county's annual operating budget for the fiscal year ending September 30 — a different fiscal calendar from the City of Houston inside the same territory, which is itself worth knowing when comparing the two.

release_schedule.note: Harris County Commissioners Court adopts the county's budget in mid-to-late September each year, just before the fiscal year (Oct 1 - Sep 30) begins. Observed adoption dates: FY2024 budget adopted Sept 19, 2023; FY2025 budget adopted Sept 19, 2024; FY2026 budget adopted Sept 24, 2025. Texas Local Gov't Code Sec. 111.039 requires a record vote at the conclusion of the public budget hearing but does not itself state a fixed calendar deadline, so this is classified as an observed pattern rather than a stated rule. The exact date within September varies year to year, so no single day is asserted for FY2027; only the month is given.

reports.title: Harris County Annual Comprehensive Financial Report
reports.description: The county's audited annual financial statements for the fiscal year ended September 30.

entries.covers: FY2026 ACFR (fiscal year ended 2026-09-30), expected next edition

release_schedule.note: Harris County's fiscal year ends September 30. No published release calendar or stated statutory deadline was found on the Auditor's site, but the last three ACFR editions were issued in late March / early April, roughly six months after fiscal year end: FY2023 ACFR issued 2024-03-28, FY2024 ACFR issued 2025-04-08, FY2025 ACFR issued 2026-04-07 (auditor's report / transmittal letter dates). The FY2025 ACFR (for FYE 2025-09-30) has already been released as of 2026-08-11, so the next expected edition is the FY2026 ACFR (for FYE 2026-09-30), projected for early April 2027 based on this pattern.

reports.title: Metropolitan Transit Authority of Harris County financial reports
reports.publisher: Metropolitan Transit Authority of Harris County
reports.description: The transit authority's annual financial reporting. Funded principally by a 1 percent sales and use tax authorised by voters in 1978, collected by the state and remitted to the authority. The counterpart to LA Metro, and unlike LA Metro its reports are not served as retrievable documents — see the _dropped entry.

entries.covers: FY2023 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (year ended 2023-09-30)
FY2024 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (year ended 2024-09-30)
FY2025 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (year ended 2025-09-30)
FY2026 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (year ending 2026-09-30)

release_schedule.note: METRO's fiscal year runs October 1 - September 30 (confirmed on the ACFR cover page: 'Fiscal Year Begins on October 1 and Ends on September 30'). The Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) for a given fiscal year is consistently issued in late March of the following calendar year, roughly 5.5-6 months after fiscal year end. Verified via PDF metadata (CreationDate) and the CFO transmittal-letter date on three consecutive editions downloaded directly from METRO's official document library (metro.resourcespace.com, linked from the corpus url): FY2023 ACFR created/dated 2024-03-22; FY2024 ACFR created 2025-03-24 (letter undated in extract but consistent); FY2025 ACFR created 2026-03-20, with its transmittal letter explicitly dated 'March 20, 2026' for 'the year ended September 30, 2025'. As of today (2026-08-11) the FY2025 ACFR is the latest published edition; the FY2026 ACFR (for the year ending 2026-09-30, not yet complete) is the next expected release, projected for March 2027 based on this three-year pattern. No published release calendar or statutory/continuing-disclosure deadline rule was found on METRO's site; the March timing is an observed pattern only.

reports.title: Reinvestment Zone No. 24, City of Houston — annual financial statements
reports.publisher: Harris County Redevelopment Authority No. 24 / City of Houston
reports.description: The audited statements of one of Houston's 27 active tax increment reinvestment zones, a component unit of the City. A zone captures the property tax revenue attributable to appraised value above a frozen base year and spends it inside its own boundary — a municipal-finance structure with no Los Angeles counterpart of comparable density.

entries.covers: FY ended Sept 30, 2022 audited financial statements (independent auditor's report dated April 14, 2023)
FY ended Sept 30, 2024 audited financial statements (independent auditor's report dated February 20, 2025; posted to site March 2025)
FY ended Sept 30, 2025 annual financial statements (next expected release)

release_schedule.note: Harris County Redevelopment Authority No. 24 / Reinvestment Zone No. 24 (a component unit of Harris County) uses a fiscal year ending September 30. Its independently audited annual financial statements have historically been issued and posted to harriscountyrda24.org roughly 4.5-6.5 months after fiscal year end (e.g., April 2023 for FY2022, February/March 2025 for FY2024), but the exact month varies year to year, so this is an observed pattern rather than a fixed rule. As of 2026-08-11, no FY2025 (year ended 9/30/2025) financial report was found linked on the publisher's financial-reports page (https://harriscountyrda24.org/tirz-24-board_meeting_information/, which lists a '2025 Financial Report' placeholder with no working link), meaning it appears overdue relative to the historical pattern; exact release date is unknown so a broad window is given. Note: this audited financial statement is distinct from the separate, simpler statutory report Texas municipalities must file under Tax Code Sec. 311.016 within 150 days of the city's fiscal year end for each TIRZ.

reports.title: Harris County Municipal Utility District No. 285 — annual audit report
reports.publisher: Harris County Municipal Utility District No. 285
reports.description: The audited annual financial report of one named municipal utility district, kept under the state water district financial management guide. Included as the concrete instance of a class that is enormous in suburban Houston and absent from every other region in this corpus: independent special districts that levy property tax and issue debt to finance water and wastewater infrastructure, each with its own fiscal year — this one ends March 31.

entries.covers: Audited annual financial statements for fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 (EMMA/MSRB continuing-disclosure filing deadline)

release_schedule.rule: Per the District's bond continuing-disclosure covenant: the District must provide to the MSRB through EMMA its continuing disclosure of annual financial information and operating data, and 'the information, along with the audited annual financial statements, must be filed within six months after the end of each fiscal year of the District.' The District's fiscal year ends March 31.
release_schedule.note: The FY2025 audit (year ended March 31, 2025) was dated July 21, 2025, well ahead of the six-month EMMA deadline. Board minutes show the audit is typically presented and approved by the Board at its mid-July meeting each year (e.g., July 15, 2024 and July 15, 2019 minutes both show audit approval), so the FY2026 audit (year ended March 31, 2026) was likely already completed and presented by the time of this research (2026-08-11), even though the formal six-month EMMA filing deadline is September 30, 2026. Could not locate a July 2026 board minutes document to confirm the exact FY2026 audit date, so the stated-rule deadline is used as the safe, evidenced 'next' date.

dependencies.basis: Tax Code §26.01(a) starts the chain: "By July 25, the chief appraiser shall prepare and certify to the assessor for each taxing unit participating in the district that part of the appraisal roll for the district that lists the property taxable by the unit." §26.04(b) continues it: "The assessor shall submit the appraisal roll for the taxing unit ... to the governing body of the taxing unit by August 1 or as soon thereafter as practicable." The certified roll is the denominator of every rate the City then calculates.

reference_period.stated_as: Values as of the January 1 appraisal date, certified by July 25 in statute — though Harris Central certified on 16 August in 2024, so the statutory date is a floor rather than a description.

dependencies.basis: Tax Code §26.04(c) gives the formulas verbatim: "NO-NEW-REVENUE TAX RATE = (LAST YEAR'S LEVY - LOST PROPERTY LEVY) / (CURRENT TOTAL VALUE - NEW PROPERTY VALUE)", and "VOTER-APPROVAL TAX RATE = (NO-NEW-REVENUE MAINTENANCE AND OPERATIONS RATE x 1.035) + (CURRENT DEBT RATE + UNUSED INCREMENT RATE)" for ordinary taxing units. The Comptroller frames the purpose: truth-in-taxation "requires local taxing units to make taxpayers aware of tax rate proposals and to afford taxpayers the opportunity to limit tax increases", and the voter-approval rate is "a calculated maximum rate allowed by law without voter approval".

The same certification under Tax Code §26.01(a) runs to every taxing unit in the district, the county included. Harris Central's annual report states that the district "provides each taxing unit with a list of its taxable property, together with the January 1 value of each property", and that "The appraisal roll was certified on August 16, 2024, with less than 4.74 percent of the total appraised value in the district remaining under protest."

reference_period.stated_as: Values as of the January 1 appraisal date.

dependencies.basis: Chapter 26 governs every Texas taxing unit, not only cities. The county computes the same no-new-revenue and voter-approval rates from the same certified roll, with the 3.5 percent multiplier for ordinary units, and must hold an election to exceed the voter-approval rate.

Tax Code §23.23(a): "an appraisal office may increase the appraised value of a residence homestead for a tax year to an amount not to exceed the lesser of: (1) the market value of the property for the most recent tax year that the market value was determined by the appraisal office; or (2) the sum of: (A) 10 percent of the appraised value of the property for the preceding tax year; (B) the appraised value of the property for the preceding tax year; and (C) the market value of all new improvements to the property." §23.23(c) attaches the limitation on January 1 of the year after the owner first qualifies for a homestead exemption and expires it when neither that owner nor a surviving spouse still qualifies.

reference_period.stated_as: The preceding tax year's appraised value, against market value determined as of January 1.

dependencies.basis: Government Code §403.302(a): "The comptroller shall conduct a study using comparable sales and generally accepted auditing and sampling techniques to determine the total taxable value of all property in each school district." The study tests each appraisal district's values: under §403.302(c) a local value found valid "is presumed to represent taxable value for the school district", and where it is invalid the state value is used instead unless the local value is the higher of the two, with validity judged against a margin of error not exceeding 5 percent.

The study exists because §403.302 requires it, and the section also fixes its publication and certification: "The comptroller shall publish preliminary findings, listing values by district, before February 1 of the year following the year of the study ... Preliminary findings shall be delivered to each school district and shall be certified to the commissioner of education."

reference_period.stated_as: Preliminary findings before February 1 of the year following the study year, then final findings after the protest period. The statutory floor is a study at least once every two years.

dependencies.basis: The Agency's data elements and timelines document states it plainly: "Property values are received from the Comptroller's Property Value Study (PVS) and are used for determining each district's local share of Tier One funding", with local property estimate values "updated in February / March with preliminary PVS results from the Comptroller" and the near-final and final runs "updated with final PVS results from the Comptroller". The school finance overview corroborates the routing: "TEA obtains information on district property values and tax rates from the Property Tax Assistance Division of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts." This is the load-bearing edge of the Texas system — state aid is computed on the audited value, not the appraisal district's.

reference_period.stated_as: Read twice a year: preliminary study results in February and March, final results at the near-final and final settlement runs.

dependencies.evidence_quote: updated in February / March with preliminary PVS results from the Comptroller

dependencies.basis: The Agency's annual letter setting maximum compressed rates states that it uses "preliminary state-certified property values from the Comptroller's Property Tax Assistance Division", under Education Code §§48.2551 and 48.2552 and 19 Texas Administrative Code §61.1000. Rate compression is driven by property value growth, so the audited value determines not only how much state aid a district receives but the rate it is permitted to levy.

Article III §49a(b) supplies the binding force the two estimates share: "no appropriation in excess of the cash and anticipated revenue of the funds from which such appropriation is to be made shall be valid" except on a four-fifths vote of both chambers, and "No bill containing an appropriation shall be considered as passed or be sent to the Governor for consideration until and unless the Comptroller of Public Accounts endorses his certificate thereon showing that the amount appropriated is within the amount estimated to be available." The Biennial Revenue Estimate sets the ceiling before the session; the Certification Revenue Estimate updates it and is what the certification endorsement is measured against.
dependencies.evidence_quote: No bill containing an appropriation shall be considered as passed or be sent to the Governor for consideration until and unless the Comptroller of Public Accounts endorses his certificate thereon showing that the amount appropriated is within the amount estimated to be available in the affected funds. When the Comptroller finds an appropriation bill exceeds the estimated revenue he shall endorse such finding thereon and return to the House in which same originated.

dependencies.basis: The transfer is computed against actual net production tax collections, which the Comptroller reports monthly by revenue source. Article III §49-g(d) fixes the comparison: "If in the preceding year the state received from oil production taxes a net amount greater than the net amount of oil production taxes received by the state in the fiscal year ending August 31, 1987, the comptroller shall transfer to the economic stabilization fund an amount equal to 75 percent of the difference between those amounts. The comptroller shall retain the remaining 25 percent of the difference as general revenue." §49-g(e) is the parallel provision for gas.

reference_period.stated_as: Net collections for the preceding fiscal year, against the fiscal 1987 baseline. Oil and gas are two separate computations with separate baselines, so one can trigger while the other does not.

dependencies.basis: Article III §49-g(c-1) splits the resulting amount: "the comptroller shall allocate one-half to the economic stabilization fund and the remainder to the state highway fund." §49-g(g) caps the destination: "During each fiscal biennium, the amount in the economic stabilization fund may not exceed an amount equal to 10 percent of the total amount, excluding investment income, interest income, and amounts borrowed from special funds, deposited in general revenue during the preceding biennium." The cap now binds — the Comptroller reports that the fund would have received about $5.1 billion from severance taxes in 2026-27 without it, and receives nothing in 2027, while the highway fund is unaffected.

Article VII §5(a)(1) sets the ceiling and the window: the distribution "in each year of a state fiscal biennium must be an amount that is not more than six percent of the average of the market value of the permanent school fund, excluding real property belonging to the fund that is managed, sold, or acquired under Section 4 of this article, on the last day of each of the 16 state fiscal quarters preceding the regular session of the legislature that begins before that state fiscal biennium, in accordance with the rate adopted by" the State Board of Education. §5(a)(2) adds the long-run test: distributions over the current and nine preceding fiscal years "may not exceed the total return on all investment assets of the permanent school fund over the same 10-year period".

reference_period.stated_as: The average market value on the last day of each of the 16 fiscal quarters preceding the regular session before the biennium — so the valuation window closes well before the money is distributed.

dependencies.basis: The valuation states: "The actuarial methods and assumptions are primarily based on a study of actual experience for the period ending August 31, 2021 and adopted on July 15, 2022." The experience study for its part covers "the four-year period from August 31, 2021 through August 31, 2025" and "includes our recommendations for new actuarial assumptions to be effective for the August 31, 2026 actuarial valuation."

reference_period.stated_as: A four-year experience window. Note the phase: the August 2025 valuation still runs on assumptions adopted in July 2022 from the study ending August 2021; the February 2026 study does not take effect until the August 2026 valuation.

dependencies.evidence_quote: The actuarial methods and assumptions are primarily based on a study of actual experience for the period ending August 31, 2021 and adopted on July 15, 2022.

dependencies.basis: The valuation states: "The assumptions and methods applied in this actuarial valuation were adopted by the Board of Trustees on March 20, 2024 based on the experience investigation that covered the period ending August 31, 2023." The study itself covers "the four-year period from August 31, 2020 through August 31, 2023" with assumptions "effective for the August 31, 2024 actuarial valuation" — so unlike the teacher system, the state employee valuation and its experience study are in phase.

reference_period.stated_as: A four-year experience window, adopted for the valuation two years after the window closes.

dependencies.basis: The City's budget states the sourcing in a footnote to the cap calculation: "CPI increase based on the change in the CPI-U for Houston-The Woodlands-Sugar Land, Texas as published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, for the preceding calendar year", and reports applying "the 2024 inflation rate of 2.4641%". Note the standing this has: the charter language as quoted in the City's own bond disclosure says only "inflation", so naming this particular series is the Finance Department's documented implementation rather than a charter definition.

reference_period.stated_as: The change in the index for the preceding calendar year, read as an annual average — which is what makes a bimonthly series usable.

dependencies.basis: The same footnote: "Population numbers based upon the US Census Bureau estimate most recently published when deciding limits of each respective year's property tax revenue budget increase", with the City reporting "population estimates as of July 1, 2024 of 3.28%". The charter text as quoted in the City's financial report says "the City's population growth (as determined by the U.S. Census)", so the specific series is again the administrative implementation.

reference_period.stated_as: The most recently published July 1 estimate at the time the limit is set.

dependencies.evidence_quote: population estimates as of July 1, 2024 of 3.28%

dependencies.basis: The cap fixes the property tax revenue the budget may assume, and the City's own bond disclosure states the formula: Proposition 1 limits increases "by requiring voter approval for increases in ad valorem taxes in future years above a limit equal to the lesser of the actual revenues in the preceding Fiscal Year, plus 4.5%, or a formula that is based upon the actual revenues received in Fiscal Year 2005 adjusted for the cumulative combined rates of inflation and the City's population growth". The same Official Statement records the 2006 amendment allowing the City "to collect and spend up to $90 million of revenue, over and above any Proposition 2 limitations, for increased police, fire and emergency medical services". Note the second branch adjusts a fiscal 2005 base cumulatively, not the prior year's cap.

The revenue cap appears in the first note of the City's audited statements, in the terms the bond market relies on, and the same language is reproduced in the City's general obligation bond official statements. That the cap is described in the financial statements rather than only in the budget is what makes it a durable constraint rather than a budgeting convention.

The authority's 1 percent rate is set under Transportation Code §451.404, which permits a board to impose the tax "at the rate of: (1) one-quarter of one percent; (2) one-half of one percent; (3) three-quarters of one percent; or (4) one percent", and the Comptroller lists the Houston authority at 1 percent effective 1 October 1978. Collection and remittance sit in Tax Code Chapter 322, not Chapter 451: §322.201(a) "The comptroller shall administer, collect, and enforce the sales and use tax of a taxing entity", §322.302 requires remittance "at least quarterly during each state fiscal year and as often as feasible", and §322.303 deducts "two percent of the amount of the taxes collected ... as the state's charge for its services".

A zone captures the tax attributable to appraised value above a frozen base. Tax Code §311.016 requires the annual report to state "the tax increment base and current captured appraised value retained by the zone", along with "the amount and source of revenue in the tax increment fund established for the zone" and "the amount and purpose of expenditures from the fund", filed "on or before the 150th day following the end of the fiscal year of the municipality or county" with a copy to the Comptroller. The captured value is a direct function of the appraisal district's roll.

reference_period.stated_as: Captured appraised value against a frozen base year, on the January 1 appraisal date; reported within 150 days of fiscal year end.

dependencies.basis: The district's audit states that it "maintains accounting records generally in accordance with the Water District Financial Management Guide published by the Commission" — the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality. The auditor's opinion is that the statements "present fairly, in all material respects, the respective financial position of the governmental activities and each major fund of the District as of March 31, 2025 ... in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America."

_dropped.why: A negative finding and a clean contrast. California requires the state to determine each region's housing need and each council of governments to allocate it among cities, which puts `ca-hcd-rhna-determination` and `scag-rhna-allocation-plan` in the graph. Texas has no statewide or regional housing allocation mandate, and Houston has no zoning ordinance at all, so there is nothing to model. The absence is the comparison.

_dropped.edge: texas -> any Proposition 13 equivalent statewide value cap
_dropped.why: Recorded so the asymmetry is legible rather than looking like missing research. Texas constrains the rate, not the value: Chapter 26's no-new-revenue and voter-approval rates with a 3.5 percent multiplier for ordinary units, and a separate compressed-rate regime for school districts. The only broad value cap is §23.23's 10 percent homestead limitation, which is narrower on three counts — homesteads only, appraised rather than market value, and it expires when the qualifying owner does. California caps what a property is worth; Texas caps what a jurisdiction may charge.

_dropped.edge: houston-revenue-cap -> the City Charter text itself
_dropped.why: The operative charter language could not be retrieved from any static source. Houston's charter is served only through Municode's JavaScript viewer, which returns no body text to any fetcher, the Municode API endpoints 404, and no city-published PDF exists at any tested path. Every retrievable source — the annual financial report, the budget, the bond official statement, and the litigation over the cap — paraphrases rather than quotes. The charter section number is likewise unconfirmed. Consequence for the two edges above: the CPI and Census series they name are documented as the Finance Department's implementation, not as charter definitions, and the basis text says so.

The transit authority publishes no retrievable financial statements. Every document link on its finance page points into a JavaScript-gated asset manager that returns only a browser check to any fetcher, and there is no direct URL for its annual comprehensive financial report. The reliable path is continuing-disclosure filings on the municipal securities board's EMMA system. Worth contrasting with LA Metro, whose budget is a plain PDF: same kind of body, same kind of document, one publishable and one not.

Rejected as proposed. A generic aggregate of municipal utility district financials is not a report and cannot be a node — the districts have different fiscal year ends (No. 285 ends March 31, others vary), separate auditors and separate statements. Replaced with one named district. The systematic channel, per that district's own audit note, is EMMA: the district "is required to provide to the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board ... through its Electronic Municipal Market Access system (EMMA) continuing disclosure of certain annual financial information and operating data", within six months of year end. A future pass wanting coverage rather than an instance should go to EMMA, not to district websites.

The Houston Independent School District budget was proposed as a node and is not minted here: no verified URL and no documented statement of its funding inputs was obtained. The district is under state intervention, which may make its funding documentation unusually explicit, so it is worth a dedicated pass. Note the same failure mode already recorded for Los Angeles Unified — school district budget sites are consistently the least publishable documents in this corpus.

_dropped.edge: comptroller-esf-transfer -> a severance tax summary page
_dropped.why: The Comptroller's Severance Taxes page looks like the right source and is not: it is a static explainer last revised in October 2022, still reporting fiscal 2022 as the record year. The live series is the Monthly State Revenue Watch, which is what the edge points at. Recorded because the wrong page is the one a search returns first.

_dropped.edge: ESF transfer as a single combined oil-and-gas threshold
_dropped.why: A correction to the research this slice was built from, kept so it is not reintroduced. Three things were wrong in the original account. Oil and gas are two separate transfers under §49-g(d) and (e) with separate fiscal 1987 baselines, so one can trigger while the other does not. The 25 percent the state retains goes to general revenue, not to the highway fund — the highway fund's share comes from splitting the 75 percent afterwards under (c-1). And the $531.9 million and $599.8 million baseline figures are Comptroller-published, not constitutional text; the Constitution names only the fiscal year.

_dropped.edge: the PVS as an unconditional override of local appraisal
_dropped.why: Another correction carried forward. The state value does not simply replace an invalid local value: under §403.302(c) a valid local value "is presumed to represent taxable value for the school district", and where the local value is invalid the state value applies unless the local value is the higher of the two. Validity is judged against a margin of error not exceeding 5 percent. The override is conditional and asymmetric, which matters because the asymmetry always favours the larger number and therefore less state aid.

The county's audited statements plainly rest on the certified appraisal roll — the property tax note in any Texas county ACFR describes the January 1 lien and the levy — but the notes to the financial statements were not read this pass, so nothing could be quoted. The node is therefore an intentional island for now. The same gap was recorded for the City of Los Angeles ACFR in the California pass, and it is the same fix in both cases: read the property tax note.
